rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥāqqah resembles the preceding al-Wāqiʿah in affirming the Resurrection and depicting its terrors.
rows.anchor: both substantiate the Day of Judgement and portray the horrors of that Day.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both sūrahs describe the outcomes for the companions of the right and left hands.
rows.anchor: both mention the details of the fate met by the companions of the right hand

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both sūrahs swear to the Qur’an’s veracity and genuineness.
rows.anchor: the veracity and genuineness of the Qur’ān is sworn by.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥāqqah shares al-Qalam’s central theme, substantiating the Day of Judgement, though their arguments differ.
rows.anchor: Its central theme is the same as that of the previous sūrah: substantiation of the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qalam discusses the Qur’an’s greatness and truth and warns against rejecting it near its opening; al-Ḥāqqah places this subject at its conclusion, a useful variation for instruction and reminder.
rows.anchor: in the previous sūrah, it is discussed in the opening part while in this sūrah, in the concluding part.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–12 cite earlier nations as evidence that rejecting messengers brings certain punishment in this world and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The history of various nations is cited as evidence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 13–18 portray the terrors of the Day of Judgement.
rows.anchor: a portrayal of the horrors of the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 19–37 detail the destinies of the companions of the right and left hands.
rows.anchor: details of the fate met by the companions of the right hand and by the companions of the left hand.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 38–52 affirm the Qur’an’s exaltedness and truth, reject its attribution to a poet or soothsayer, identify its noble messenger, and warn deniers to consider the consequences.
rows.anchor: a mention of the exaltedness and veracity of the Qur’ ān; it is not the work of a poet or a soothsayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥāqqah names an event certain to occur according to common sense and morality; it is inevitable.
rows.anchor: bound to happen as per the dictates of common sense and morality; something which is inevitable and certain to materialize.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word al-Ḥāqqah substitutes for an entire sentence.
rows.anchor: This one word is actually a substitute for the whole sentence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treating mā al-Ḥāqqah as the predicate is an erroneous grammatical analysis.
rows.anchor: to be its khabar (enunciative) have made an erroneous conclusion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The truncated, ambiguous wording jolts an indifferent addressee by focusing attention on the opening subject and drawing attention through uncertainty.
rows.anchor: The khabar is not mentioned so that all the attention of the addressee is focused on the mubtadā’.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a name for the Day of Judgement, al-Ḥāqqah conveys both its certainty and why it must occur.
rows.anchor: This name not only expresses the certainty of its happening but why it should necessarily happen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rational and moral arguments for the Day’s necessity are explained in earlier sūrahs, with indications also in this and later sūrahs.
rows.anchor: The arguments of both these aspects can also be seen in the exegesis of the previous sūrahs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥāqqah secondarily includes the inevitable punishment nations face for rejecting their messenger.
rows.anchor: also included in it in a secondary manner is the punishment which a nation necessarily faces if it rejects its messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishment for rejecting a messenger prefigures and substantiates the Hereafter’s punishment because it follows rejection of that Day.
rows.anchor: this punishment is a prelude to the punishment on the Day of Judgement and also its substantiation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers warn of both the Hereafter and the punishment that follows denial; after the truth is conclusively conveyed, deniers’ punishment arrives, and every divine promise and messenger’s warning is true.
rows.anchor: every warning of the messenger is true, hence, this punishment also is

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā al-Ḥāqqah heightens dread: who can know what this inevitable event is and what will befall its stubborn deniers?
rows.anchor: is a powerful expression of the horror and dreadfulness which is further explained by the subsequent words:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same startling mode of address appears in al-Qāriʿah, where the author says he will explain it further.
rows.anchor: In Sūrah al-Qāri‘ah also, this style of address can be witnessed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ṭāghiyah means something exceeding its bounds; God turns life-serving forces into destroyers when people exceed limits, as Thamūd did in rebellion.
rows.anchor: the Almighty punishes a people according to their attitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an calls Noah’s floodwater ṭaghā al-māʾ and says Thamūd denied because of rebellion.
rows.anchor: the rain water in which the people of Noah (sws) were drowned is called

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the sūrah leaves Thamūd’s calamity unnamed, Qur’anic indications discussed in al-Dhāriyāt suggest a thunderbolt from striped winter clouds.
rows.anchor: by a thunderbolt which appeared from the striped winter clouds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ordinary lightning bolt can become a weapon of destruction by God’s will, and modern scientific advances do not remove humanity’s helplessness before Him.
rows.anchor: whenever the Almighty wants, He brings to the fore the helplessness of all the scientists of the world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘Ād were destroyed by tempestuous winter winds; ʿātiyah names an uncontrollable wind, paralleling Thamūd’s ṭāghiyah.
rows.anchor: were routed by tempestuous winter winds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind ordinarily serves human life, but God transforms it into death and destruction when people rebel.
rows.anchor: when man becomes rebellious, He transforms this docile wind into an instrument of death and destruction.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥasm and ḥusūm mean ravaging and destroying.
rows.anchor: mean “to ravage and destroy.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address “you would have seen” is general and refers to no particular person.
rows.anchor: The address “you would have seen” on such instances is general and does not refer to someone specific.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-qawm means opponents or adversaries here, aptly portraying the rebellious ‘Ād as God’s opponents.
rows.anchor: here refers to “opponents and adversaries.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment knocked the ‘Ād down like hollow palm trunks blown about by wind.
rows.anchor: the punishment of God knocked them to the ground as if they were hollow trunks of palm-trees, which are blown away here and

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive pronoun in fīhā can refer either to the wind or to the land inhabited by the ‘Ād; both are linguistically possible.
rows.anchor: can be the wind as well as the land in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about whether anyone remains continues the previous verse’s taraa and makes the ruined ‘Ād’s fate vivid to the audience.
rows.anchor: the fate of the settlements of the ‘ Ād is brought before the imagination of the addressees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question implies that punishment utterly ravages a people; those foolishly demanding to see it should seek refuge from it.
rows.anchor: it is not something to be seen – it is something to be sought refuge from.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muʾtafikah refers to Lot’s overturned settlements, ruined by earthquake and covered by a stone-bearing wind with sand and pebbles.
rows.anchor: Here, it refers to the places inhabited by the nation of Lot (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh could often see the remains of Lot’s settlements.
rows.anchor: The Quraysh were often able to see the remnants of these people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot’s people met the same fate as ‘Ād and Thamūd because they shared the same crime.
rows.anchor: They too met a similar fate as the people of ‘ Ād and the Tham ūd since both had committed the same crime.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger is the universe’s King’s envoy, so disobeying him is rebellion that merits a rebel’s punishment.
rows.anchor: A messenger of God is an envoy of the King of the universe.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akhdhatan rābiyatan is an indefensible, unbearable seizure, unlike a temporary punishment meant to warn and remind.
rows.anchor: One type of God’s punishment is that which is only meant to warn and remind people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s people are included last in the list though they were historically the first nation mentioned to face God’s wrath, briefly evoking the history of the messengers.
rows.anchor: Historically, they were the first among those nations mentioned to have faced the wrath of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh are reminded that their ancestors were rescued in Noah’s ark because they believed in God’s messenger; as Noah’s descendants they indirectly received that favor and must remember history.
rows.anchor: the people whose descendents they are, were given refuge in the ark of Noah (sws) by the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Quraysh forget this favor and disobey their messenger, God may deal with them as He dealt with Noah’s people.
rows.anchor: there is no reason why the Almighty not deal with them in the very manner He dealt with the people of Noah (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “to make it a reminder” refers to the whole account of divine reward and punishment, not merely the ark.
rows.anchor: is not merely the ark; it is in fact the whole account of God’s reward and punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account was meant to teach Noah’s survivors, be transmitted to later generations, and remain in memory; people forgot it and rebelled like Noah’s nation.
rows.anchor: make them remember it, learn a lesson from it and to transmit it to their later generations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Just as God needs no elaborate arrangements to punish nations, one trumpet blast suffices to bring the Day’s upheaval.
rows.anchor: one blow of the trumpet would be enough to signal this great upheaval to take place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can take up the earth and mountains and shatter them together in one collision; their scale poses no obstacle to Him.
rows.anchor: with one collision He will shatter them to pieces.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers mockingly asked whether Judgement could pound the mountains apart, reasoning that such an impossible event would never occur.
rows.anchor: they would mockingly inquire if the Day of Judgement would also pound these mountains to pieces.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What deniers deem improbable will certainly appear.
rows.anchor: what these disbelievers are regarding as improbable will one day definitely manifest itself.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name al-Wāqiʿah presents Judgement as an event bound to occur, whether or not anyone thinks it improbable; the sūrah has also called it al-Ḥāqqah and al-Qāriʿah.
rows.anchor: to God it is something which is bound to happen.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky, now apparently solid, will become frail and brittle, flying apart like smoke and pieces of cotton.
rows.anchor: on that Day it will be frail and brittle, and will fly like smoke and cotton pieces.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The upheaval frightens the angels; this counters idolaters’ hopes that angels would help or intercede, as all but the eight throne-bearers withdraw.
rows.anchor: idolaters who believed that angels would help them and intercede for them on the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Descriptions of Judgement are mutashābihāt, using familiar words to give a broad understanding of an unseen reality whose true form cannot be known.
rows.anchor: The happenings and incidents mentioned by the Qur’ān which will take place on the Day of Judgement are from among the mutashābihāt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers should accept these descriptions broadly as given and avoid probing their exact form, lest they fall into a trial.
rows.anchor: they should not go after knowing their exact form, lest they might end up in some trial.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being brought forth means before God; after the heavens and earth are destroyed, no place or thing can hide a person.
rows.anchor: the heavens and the earth shall be destroyed; so a person will not have any place to hide himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer rejoices on receiving his record and asks others to read it.
rows.anchor: A believer will jump with joy when he sees his account and will ask others to read it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hā is an interjection like “ah” or “oh,” used to present or call attention to something; um merely fills the gap before the following word.
rows.anchor: sound similar to “ah” or “oh;” it is used when the speaker wants to say: “take hold of this.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word um is superfluous filler, with parallels in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: Examples of such superfluous words can be seen in previous sūrahs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The h in kitābiyah is a saktah marker added to fit the rhyme, with parallels in earlier and later sūrahs.
rows.anchor: is for saktah which has come in consideration of the rhyme of the previous verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The successful believer explains his joy by saying he expected one day to account for his deeds; this expectation kept him from evil.
rows.anchor: he always thought that one day he will have to give an account of his deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓann here means a probable thought or belief, supported by signs in the world, within oneself, and in prophetic and wise teachings; conscience testifies that the world will not simply end and accountability will come.
rows.anchor: There exist potent signs and indications in the world around man, in that within him and in the teachings of the prophets and sages

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A likely belief in accountability strengthens toward certainty through experience; waiting to believe until Judgement is seen makes faith useless.
rows.anchor: reaches the stage of certitude. If a person ignores this “likely belief” and thinks

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessed will live in ecstasy in a lofty garden whose low-hanging fruit is readily accessible.
rows.anchor: the orchards will be on high ground yet their fruits – which is what is really required from them – will be accessible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For Arab orchards, date-palms at the edges and pomegranate and grape trees at the center illustrate the contrast between lofty gardens and reachable fruit; height and accessible fruit make an orchard beautiful.
rows.anchor: date-palms would be grown on the edges while in the centre there would be pomegranate-trees and grape wines.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hereafter’s eating and drinking are always beneficial, unlike worldly favors that can harm without balance or gratitude.
rows.anchor: the favours of the next world afford no such danger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What you sent ahead” means the deeds of the worldly life earned this reward; the work is done, its benefits are everlasting, and may increase without diminishing.
rows.anchor: the favours they have received in this world are a reward for their deeds done in the previous world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers readers to al-Ṭūr for the linguistic analysis of hanīʾan.
rows.anchor: has already been presented in S ūrah al-Ṭūr.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in yā laytahā refers to death; contextual indication permits this pronoun use, as in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: The antecedent in the pronoun in ﻳٰﻠﻴۡﺘﻬﺎ is “death.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā can be negative or interrogative; the author prefers the question because it expresses yearning and longing.
rows.anchor: I would prefer its latter meaning because in this case it would express yearning and longing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ʿan after halaka makes the verb carry the sense of going away or disappearing.
rows.anchor: shows that the latter encompasses the meaning of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sulṭān means authority; the speaker longs for the loss of worldly authority that had made him arrogant and heedless of Judgement.
rows.anchor: They will longingly express the loss of the authority they had in the previous world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who hoarded wealth by counting it will be chained to columns so they feel the heat of flames from the treasures they guarded; the author promises more detail in al-Humazah.
rows.anchor: those who amassed wealth by counting and hoarding it will be tied to columns through heavy chains

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship of wealth and regret that it is useless reveal disbelief: a believer would fear accounting for wealth and recognize that none can rescue anyone from God.
rows.anchor: his attitude of worshipping wealth in the previous world and his yearning that this wealth was of no use to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wealthy miser neither feeds the poor nor urges others to do so, wanting to hide his own stinginess; al-Māʿūn makes the same charge against one who drives away orphans and fails to urge feeding the poor.
rows.anchor: In Sūrah al-Mā’ūn, the words used are:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taken together, al-Māʿūn’s description of neglectful, showy prayer and stinginess shows that wealthy people who refuse help to orphans and needy people have no real faith or prayer, despite their claims.
rows.anchor: the faith and prayers of those who in spite of having wealth do not help the orphans and the needy have no value

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person who denied God’s and creatures’ rights has no sympathizer in the Hereafter; even stingy rich people lack sympathizers in this life.
rows.anchor: those who are stingy in spite of being wealthy have no sympathizers in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Selfish wealth, spent on personal pleasure while usurping the poor’s rights, becomes filth; spending wealth for God purifies it, while unspent wealth’s real form appears as foul food in Judgement.
rows.anchor: and this greed made their wealth filthy by usurping the rights of the poor and the indigent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only sinners receive this food, probably because their particular sin warrants a particular punishment; punishment resembling the sin is also indicated in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: since their sin was a specific one, their punishment will also be specific.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle lā before the oath is neither redundant nor a negation of the oath; it introduces the oath to refute the opponents’ claim.
rows.anchor: it comes before an oath to refute the
